q: Explain the JavaScript event loop.
a: JS has one call stack. Async callbacks wait in queues and move to the stack when it is empty. Microtasks (promises) run before macrotasks (setTimeout).

q: var vs let vs const?
a: var is function-scoped and hoisted as undefined. let and const are block-scoped with a temporal dead zone. const blocks reassignment, not mutation.

q: What is a closure?
a: A function that keeps access to variables from the scope where it was defined, even after that scope has finished. Used for private state, factories and callbacks.

q: useEffect vs useMemo in React?
a: useEffect runs side effects after render, with cleanup and a dependency array. useMemo caches a computed value until its dependencies change.

q: Why do list items need keys in React?
a: Stable unique keys let React match items between renders, so it updates or reorders them instead of remounting. Avoid array indexes if the list can change.

q: Flexbox vs Grid?
a: Flexbox lays out in one dimension (row or column). Grid handles rows and columns together. Flexbox suits components, Grid suits page layouts.

q: How do you improve web performance?
a: Split and shrink bundles, lazy-load, size and compress images, use a CDN and caching, avoid layout thrashing, and measure Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS).

q: REST vs GraphQL?
a: REST exposes resources through URLs and HTTP verbs. GraphQL lets clients ask for exactly the fields they need from one endpoint. It cuts over-fetching but complicates caching.

q: What does idempotent mean for an API?
a: Repeating a request has the same effect as sending it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by design. For POST, use idempotency keys stored server-side.

q: Authentication vs authorization? JWT pitfalls?
a: AuthN proves who you are; AuthZ decides what you may do. JWTs are stateless but hard to revoke, so use short expiry plus refresh tokens and keep secrets out of the payload.

q: What is the N+1 query problem?
a: One query loads a list, then one extra query runs per item. Fix with joins, batch loading or eager fetching (JOIN FETCH in JPA).

q: How do you handle race conditions?
a: Use transactions with suitable isolation, optimistic locking (version column) or pessimistic locks, atomic operations, and idempotent consumers.

q: How would you implement rate limiting?
a: Token bucket or sliding window per user or IP, enforced at the gateway or with Redis counters. Return 429 with a Retry-After header.

q: Monolith vs microservices?
a: A monolith is simpler to build and deploy. Microservices scale and deploy independently but add network failures, distributed data and ops cost. Start simple, split on clear boundaries.

q: Android activity lifecycle?
a: onCreate, onStart, onResume, onPause, onStop, onDestroy. Rotation and process death recreate activities, so keep UI state in a ViewModel or saved state.

q: What is recomposition in Jetpack Compose?
a: Compose re-runs only the composables that read changed state. Hoist state, use remember and stable types to avoid unnecessary recomposition.

q: What is a retain cycle in iOS?
a: ARC frees an object when strong references reach zero. Two objects (or a closure and self) holding each other strongly never free. Break it with weak or unowned references.

q: Native vs Flutter vs React Native vs KMP?
a: Native gives the best platform fidelity. Flutter and React Native share UI code. KMP shares business logic and optionally UI. Choose by team skills, performance needs and time to market.

q: How do you design an offline-first app?
a: Make a local database (Room, Core Data) the source of truth, sync in the background, queue writes, define conflict rules and retry with backoff.

q: How do you reduce app startup time and size?
a: Lazy-init, move heavy work off the main thread, use R8 and app bundles, compress assets and add baseline profiles.

q: Mobile security basics?
a: Store secrets in Keystore or Keychain, encrypt local data, pin certificates, keep keys out of the binary, obfuscate, and validate deep links.

q: What does ACID mean?
a: Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: data stays valid. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere. Durability: committed data survives crashes.

q: SQL vs NoSQL?
a: SQL gives a fixed schema, joins and strong consistency. NoSQL gives flexible schemas and easy horizontal scale with trade-offs. Choose by access patterns.

q: Normalization vs denormalization?
a: Normalizing removes redundancy and update anomalies. Denormalizing duplicates data to speed reads, at the cost of keeping copies consistent.

q: Transaction isolation levels?
a: Read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, serializable. Higher levels prevent dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, then phantoms, with less concurrency.

q: How do you optimize a slow query?
a: Read the EXPLAIN plan, add or fix indexes, avoid SELECT *, filter early, do not wrap indexed columns in functions, and paginate.

q: Common caching strategies?
a: Cache-aside, write-through and write-back, with TTLs and invalidation. Watch for stampedes and stale data. Redis is a common choice.

q: Docker container vs virtual machine?
a: Containers share the host kernel, so they are lighter and start faster. VMs run a full guest OS and isolate more strongly.

q: Stages of a CI/CD pipeline?
a: Commit, build, unit tests, static analysis, package, deploy to staging, integration tests, then a gated production deploy with rollback.

q: Pod, Deployment and Service in Kubernetes?
a: A Pod runs containers. A Deployment manages replicas and rollouts. A Service gives pods a stable network endpoint.

q: Blue-green vs canary deployment?
a: Blue-green switches all traffic between two full environments. Canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version first to catch problems early.

q: What is Infrastructure as Code?
a: Infrastructure defined in versioned files (Terraform, CloudFormation) so environments are reproducible, reviewable and automated.

q: Logs, metrics and traces?
a: Logs record events, metrics show trends for alerting, and traces follow one request across services. Together they speed up root-cause analysis.

q: Design a URL shortener.
a: Generate unique IDs (base62 counter or hash), store id-to-URL in a key-value store, cache hot links, redirect with 301 or 302, add rate limits and analytics.

q: How do you scale a system horizontally?
a: Stateless services behind a load balancer, shared cache, read replicas then sharding, async queues, and a CDN for static content.

q: Explain the CAP theorem.
a: In a network partition you must choose consistency or availability. Many systems tune this per feature, using eventual consistency where it is acceptable.

q: When do you use a message queue?
a: To decouple producers and consumers, absorb traffic spikes, retry failures and run async work. Kafka suits streams; RabbitMQ or SQS suit task queues.

q: Load balancing algorithms?
a: Round robin, least connections, IP hash and weighted variants. L4 routes on network info, L7 on HTTP content.

q: How do you approach a system design question?
a: Clarify requirements and scale, estimate load, sketch the high-level design, deep-dive bottlenecks, then discuss trade-offs and failure modes.

q: Unit vs integration vs end-to-end tests?
a: Unit tests isolate one piece, integration tests check components together, e2e tests run full user flows. Keep many unit tests and fewer e2e (test pyramid).

q: Mock vs stub?
a: A stub returns canned data. A mock also verifies interactions, such as which calls were made.

q: What should you automate?
a: Stable, repetitive, high-risk regression paths. Keep exploratory testing and one-off checks manual.

q: What makes a test flaky and how do you fix it?
a: Shared state, timing, network or order dependence. Isolate data, use deterministic waits and fakes, and quarantine then fix the test.

q: How do you test an API?
a: Check status codes, schema, auth, validation and error paths, idempotency and performance, using contract tests plus automated suites (Postman, REST Assured).

q: How do you handle an underperforming engineer?
a: Give early, specific feedback, find the cause (skill, clarity, motivation), set clear goals with support and checkpoints, and escalate only after documented effort.

q: How do you balance tech debt and features?
a: Make debt visible and costed, reserve regular capacity, tie fixes to business risk, and clean up while touching the same area.

q: How do you run effective code reviews?
a: Review correctness, clarity and risk; automate style. Keep PRs small, be specific and kind, and respond quickly.

q: How do you mentor and grow engineers?
a: Set growth goals in 1:1s, delegate stretch work with safety nets, give regular feedback and create visible opportunities.

q: How do you handle technical disagreements?
a: Hear each side, return to goals and data, prototype if cheap, then decide, commit and document the reasoning.

q: How do you estimate and reduce delivery risk?
a: Slice work small, estimate in ranges, run spikes on unknowns early, and review risks weekly.

q: Agile vs Waterfall?
a: Waterfall runs sequential phases with fixed scope. Agile delivers in short iterations and adapts to feedback. Waterfall fits stable, well-understood requirements.

q: Scrum roles and events?
a: Roles: Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers. Events: sprint, sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review, retrospective.

q: How do you manage scope creep?
a: Baseline the scope, assess each change for time, cost and risk, get stakeholder approval, and trade scope for scope.

q: Critical path and risk management?
a: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks and sets minimum duration. Track risks in a register with probability, impact, owner and mitigation.

q: Which project metrics do you track?
a: Velocity or throughput, cycle time, burndown, defect rate and milestone delivery. Use them to see trends, not to rank people.

q: How do you resolve stakeholder conflicts?
a: Clarify each priority, tie decisions to goals and constraints, explain trade-offs openly, and escalate with options when needed.

q: What are the four pillars of OOP?
a: Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism: hide state, expose behavior, reuse and specialize types, and let one interface have many implementations.

q: Abstract class vs interface?
a: An abstract class can hold state and constructors, and a class extends only one. An interface defines a contract, can have default methods, and a class can implement many.

q: How does @Transactional work and what are its pitfalls?
a: Spring wraps the bean in a proxy that starts and commits transactions. Calls from inside the same class bypass the proxy, and checked exceptions do not roll back by default.

q: How does JVM garbage collection work and how do you tune it?
a: It reclaims unreachable objects by generation. Pick a collector (G1, ZGC) for your latency or throughput goal, size the heap, and read GC logs before changing flags.

q: List vs tuple?
a: Lists are mutable. Tuples are immutable, and hashable when their items are, so they can be dict keys.

q: What is the GIL?
a: CPython lets one thread run bytecode at a time, so threads do not speed up CPU-bound code. Use multiprocessing or native extensions; threads still help with I/O.

q: What are generators and why use them?
a: Functions that yield values lazily, saving memory on large or endless streams.

q: Array vs linked list?
a: Arrays give O(1) index access and good cache locality. Linked lists give O(1) insert at a known node but O(n) lookup.

q: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list?
a: Floyd's method: a slow and a fast pointer meet if a cycle exists. O(n) time, O(1) space.

q: When do you use dynamic programming?
a: When subproblems overlap and the optimal solution builds from optimal parts. Define the state, recurrence and base cases, then memoize or tabulate.

q: What is SQL injection and how do you prevent it?
a: Untrusted input changing a query. Use parameterized queries, least-privilege database users and input validation.

q: XSS vs CSRF?
a: XSS injects script into pages; defend with output encoding and CSP. CSRF tricks a logged-in browser into sending requests; defend with SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens.

q: How do you build a threat model?
a: Map assets, entry points and trust boundaries, list threats (STRIDE), rank by risk, then assign mitigations and owners.

q: What is overfitting and how do you avoid it?
a: The model memorizes training data and fails on new data. Use more data, regularization, cross-validation and simpler models.

q: Precision vs recall?
a: Precision: of predicted positives, how many are right. Recall: of real positives, how many you found. Choose the trade-off by the cost of each error.

q: What is RAG?
a: Retrieval-augmented generation fetches relevant documents and gives them to an LLM as context, improving factual grounding without retraining.

q: Why should we hire you?
a: Match two or three of your strengths to the role's top needs, with one concrete result for each.

q: How do you approach salary negotiation?
a: Research the market range, state your range with reasons, discuss total compensation, and stay collaborative.

q: Tell me about a time you led without authority.
a: Use STAR: how you aligned people on a shared goal with data and influence, and the outcome.

q: How do you align engineering strategy with business goals?
a: Turn business outcomes into technical bets, set measurable goals, explain trade-offs to executives and review results regularly.
